query_text: Debates on whether humans are by nature self-interested or benevolent in 18th-century British moral philosophy
query_narration: Documents should focus on the question whether humans are by natures self-interested or benevolent beings. Documents should include relevant texts by Anthony Ashley Cooper, the Third Earl of Shaftesbury, Bernard Mandeville, Francis Hutcheson, Josephy Butler, Catharine Trotter Cockburn, and others. The development of these debates by subsequent authors should also be taken into consideration. Documents that discuss human nature from a purely metaphysical or epistemological point of view and that do not focus on moral questions as to whether humans are self-interested or benevolent should be excluded.

query_text: Moral Motivation in Warburton and Cockburn
query_narration: Documents should analyse William Warbuton’s and Catharine Trotter Cockburn’s views on moral motivation. Relevant documents should address questions such as what role human’s understanding of moral relations or fitnesses plays for moral motivation, what role conscience plays, or what role God’s will plays for motivating humans to act morally. Documents that do not focus on other aspects of their moral or religious views and do not substantially consider the question of what moves humans to act morally should be excluded.

query_text: Sentiments/passions and reason in moral judgement
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical debates concerning the role of sentiments or passions, on the one hand, and reason, on the other hand in moral judgement. Documents should address themes such as moral approval or disapproval and the role that  sentiments or passions as well as reason play in moral considerations. Documents focused on other areas of philosophy such as metaphysics or epistemology without any substantial relation to moral philosophy should be excluded.

query_text: Sentiments/passions as superior to reason in moral judgement
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical debates concerning the role of sentiments or passions, on the one hand, and reason, on the other hand in moral judgement. Additionally, they should select those moral views that regard sentiments or passions as superior to reason in moral judgement than reason. Relevant documents should include texts by David Hume and other philosophers that regarded sentiments or passions superior to reason in moral considerations.

query_text: Reason as superior to sentiments/passions in moral judgement
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical debates concerning the role of sentiments or passions, on the one hand, and reason, on the other hand in moral judgement. Additionally, they should select those moral views that regard reason as superior to sentiments or passions in moral judgement than reason.

query_text: The role of sympathy in moral interaction
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical accounts of sympathy and analyse what role sympathy plays in moral interaction. Documents should include relevant texts by David Hume and Adam Smith as well as documents by other philosophers that discuss sympathy in the context of moral interaction. Themes discuss may include the sharing of fellow feelings, the role of the impartial spectator, and the correction of moral sentiments. Documents that discuss sympathy in purely metaphysical terms without relation to moral questions should be excluded.

query_text: Character development in Shaftesbury’s moral philosophy
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on Shaftesbury’s views concerning character development and analyse why and how Shaftesbury regards character development as important for reaching happiness. Documents that discuss character in psychological term without any reference to moral development, happiness, goodness or moral perfection should not be considered relevant.

query_text: Shaftesbury’s influence on British moral philosophy
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on discussions of Shaftesbury’s moral philosophy by eighteenth-century British philosophers. Authors who discuss Shaftesbury’s philosophy tend to refer to Anthony Ashley Cooper, the Third Early of Shaftesbury by different names such as “Third Earl”, “Lord Shaftesbury”, or “Shaftesbury”.

query_text: Virtue and atheism
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on the question of whether atheists can be virtuous. Documents should include relevant texts by John Locke, William Warburton, Catharine Trotter Cockburn, and others. The issues discussed in the text may be questions whether atheists can acquire moral knowledge, whether atheists can be accountable for criminal actions, whether atheists can be blamed for wrongdoing, and related issues. Documents that discuss atheism from a purely religious point of view without any substantial relation to the moral questions whether atheists can act morally or be virtuous should be excluded.

query_text: Moral fitnesses in Samuel Clarke and Catharine Trotter Cockburn
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical debates concerning moral fitnesses and include texts by Samuel Clarke and Catharine Trotter Cockburn, as well as by other eighteenth-century British philosophers. Relevant themes may include questions what actions are fitting or unfitting. Documents that discuss moral questions without any specific reference to moral fitnesses or fittingness should be excluded.

query_text: Liberty in women’s philosophical writings
query_narration: Relevant document should be texts written by female philosophers and analyse how these women account for liberty or freedom and their views on absence of freedom as well as the moral significance of being free or lacking freedom. Relevant texts may discuss what freedom or liberty is, what freedom or liberty of action is, what freedom of will is, what it means to be free to philosophize, what practical obstacles to freedom exist, how lack of time can constrain freedom, how social and economic circumstances can constrain freedom.

query_text: Liberty and necessity
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical debates concerning liberty and necessity in eighteenth-century British philosophy. In these texts the terms “liberty” and “freedom” are often used interchangeably. Relevant themes may include questions of what it means to be free, what human freedom is, what it means to be free to act, whether the will is free, what kind of freedom is required for moral accountability, whether liberty and necessity can be reconciled, whether liberty and necessity exclude each other. Documents that discuss necessity in the context of physical or metaphysical debates without reference to questions concerning freedom or liberty should be excluded.

query_text: Origin of evil
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on the origin of evil and include texts by William King as well as by other British moral philosophers who responded to King’s views concerning the origin of evil. Relevant themes may include questions of what is evil, what is the origin of evil, is evil a consequence of human choice, why does God allow evil.

query_text: Moral relations to ourselves, to others, and to God
query_narration: Relevant documents should discuss moral relations to ourselves, to others or to our neighbour, and to God. Some philosophers discuss these in terms of duties and examine our duties to ourselves, our duties to others, and our duties to God. Texts that only focus on one to two of these moral relations, but not on all three should be excluded. For example, if texts only discuss moral duties to others but do not also discuss moral duties to ourselves and to God they should be regarded as not relevant.

query_text: Friendship in the context of British moral philosophy
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on friendship and should be written by eighteenth-century British moral philosophers. The texts should consider what role friendship plays in moral interaction. Relevant themes may include what friendship is, the role of friendship for acquiring happiness, the role of friendship for moral development and perfection, whether it is morally permissible to be partial towards one’s friends. Texts that comment on friendship without any engagement with broader moral questions should be excluded.

query_text: Divine law and the foundation of morality
query_narration: Relevant documents should discuss divine law as the foundation or ground of morality. The document should include texts by John Locke and other British philosophers that believe that morality is grounded on divine law. Documents that merely discuss God or religion in other contexts without substantial treatment of the question of what the foundation or ground of morality is should be excluded.

query_text: Reward and punishment as necessary for moral motivation
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on texts by eighteenth-century British moral philosophers that regard reward and punishment as necessary for moral motivation. For example, texts may discuss that reward and punishment are required to move us to act morally. Documents that discuss moral motivation in other contexts and that do not mention reward or punishment as essential for moral motivation should be excluded.

query_text: Conscience
query_narration: Relevant documents are meant to focus on the role of conscience in moral deliberations. The documents should include relevant texts by Joseph Butler, Catharine Trotter Cockburn, William Warburton, Adam Smith, and other eighteenth-century British moral philosophers. Themes may include the authority of conscience, whether conscience can motivate us to act morally, in what relation conscience stands to other principles of human nature.

query_text: Self-government, self-improvement, or self-mastery
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on views concerning self-government, self-improvement, or self-mastery and how these are relevant for personal and moral development and perfection. The documents should include texts by Astell, Shaftesbury, and other eighteenth-century British philosophers. Relevant themes may include development of one’s intellectual capacities, moral development or improvement, government of the passions, character development, reflection on one’s own character, practical exercises for moral improvement. Texts that discuss the metaphysics of the self without substantial reference to moral questions concerning self-government, self-improvement, or self-mastery should be excluded.

query_text: Mastery or government of the passions
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on philosophical views concerning the government of the passions. Themes may include advice for governing the passions, the relation between reason and the passion, changing the object of our passions, replacing one passion with a different passion, the role of reflection in governing passions.

query_text: Cultivation of habits and moral development
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on text by eighteenth-century British philosophers that argue for the importance of the cultivation of habits and how this is relevant for moral development or improvement. Texts that discuss custom or habit without clear relation to moral development or improvement should be excluded.

query_text: Religious practices and moral development
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on text by eighteenth-century British philosophers that consider religious practices such as prayer or reading of the Bible as relevant for moral development. Texts that discuss religion or God without any clear relation to moral development or improvement should be excluded.

query_text: Moral sense in Hutcheson’s moral philosophy
query_narration: Relevant documents should analyse Hutcheson’s views concerning the moral sense and reactions by other British moral philosophers to Hutcheson’s moral sense theory.

query_text: Morality and beauty
query_narration: Relevant documents should focus on texts that regard morality as similar or analogous to beauty and should include texts by Shaftesbury, Hutcheson, and other British moral philosophers. Texts that discuss beauty in the context of metaphysical, epistemic, or aesthetic consideration without considering in what ways beauty is similar to morality should be excluded.

query_text: Astell Stoicism references

Passages should also include explicit mention of "Stoic" or "Stoicism" or authors such as Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, Seneca, Cicero, Epictetus, Lipsius, or Guillaume Du Vair.

query_text: Norris longest refernces to Plato

Materials describing Norris's relationship with any of these "platonists" are also valid results.

query_text: Hutcheson intellect and moral sense

Does he describe these capacities as working together? Does he use "intellect loaded" terminology such as "reason" "judgement" "conclusion" "proposition" or "assessment" when explaining the moral sense?

query_text: Chudleigh degrees of reality or being
query_narration: The user seeks passages in which Mary Lee Chudleigh talks about degrees of being or degrees of reality, preferably the most detailed descriptions of this idea. Specifically, passages which describe the universe as an emanation from one single source, or which explain the relationships between different "levels" of being (i.e. God, rational humans, non-rational animals). Also interesting are expressions of this idea in terms of a "chain of being."

query_text: Providence and moral attitude of acceptance

Doctrine of providence expressed as: "there is some nature (N) such that N is inherent in all objects (X), and N organizes all X towards some ultimate end."

query_text: Masham and Astell contrast intellect's function in moral life
query_narration: The user seeks contrasting passages from Damaris Masham and Mary Astell that discuss the functioning of the intellect, in particular with respect to the function of the intellect in moral life. Of particular interest are passages which describe the intellect's role in moral motivation (i.e. how do intellectual judgments relate to the way in which we act). Passages should show a contrast between these two author's views.

query_text: Moral duty of character development and rational knowledge
query_narration: The user seeks passages from any author which describe a moral duty to develop our character. Of particular interest are passages focused on habit formation, repeated action, and which describe fulfillment of this duty as occuring over a long span of time. Of particular interest are passages which describe character development exclusively in terms of the acquisition of knowledge.

query_text: Virtue as self-sufficient

This means passages which describe virtue as something which can allow us to be happy independantly of God. query_text: Will and intellect hybrid relationship in moral life

In particular, authors who describe the power of the will as absolute in itself but at the same time confined by the judgements of the intellect. Of interest are passages in which the determination of the will by the intellect is acceptable because the intellect is considered internal/part of the agent. References to Aquinas and/or John Duns Scotus on this topic are especially interesting.

query_text: Contrast morality as internal vs external struggle
query_narration: The user seeks contrasting passages between authors who view the pursuit of a moral life as an internal struggle between states of the mind (like the will and intellect, or reason and sensation), and between authors who view the pursuit of moral life as a struggle against external oppositions or constraints (like the passions, political forces and social forces).

query_text: Citations or references to Lipsius's work
